claim: Tuft cells are a group of rare epithelial cells that can detect pathogenic microbes and parasites.
source: Tuft cells are a group of rare epithelial cells that can detect pathogenic microbes and parasites.

evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data including immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Gγ13-mediated signal transduction pathway is critical to tuft cells-mediated inflammation resolution and functional repair of damaged lungs.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing worse outcomes in Gng13-cKO mice.

claim: This is the first report indicating subtype-specific contributions of tuft cells to inflammation resolution and recovery.
source: To our best knowledge, it is the first report indicating subtype-specific contributions of tuft cells to the resolution and recovery.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The respiratory system has the largest surface area exposed to the external environment.
source: The respiratory system comprises the nasal cavity, airways, and lungs, and has the largest surface area exposed to the external environment.
evidence: This is a statement based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The respiratory system is constantly challenged by various stimuli including odorants, pollutants, toxins, allergens, viruses, bacteria, and fungi.
source: It is thus constantly challenged by various stimuli, ranging from odorants, pollutants, toxins, allergens, to viruses, bacteria, and fungi.
evidence: This is a statement based on general scientific knowledge about respiratory system function.

claim: SARS-CoV-1, H1N1 influenza A virus, and SARS-CoV-2 have caused pandemics.
source: The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV-1), and H1N1 influenza A virus and SARS-CoV2 have caused pandemics (Peiris, 2003; Donaldson et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Several types of epithelial cells expressing chemosensory receptors play important roles in detecting and responding to external stimuli in the respiratory system.
source: Recent studies have shown that several types of epithelial cells expressing the chemosensory receptors play important roles in detecting and responding to the external stimuli in the respiratory system (Carey and Lee, 2019; Tizzano and Finger, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tuft cells have been found in the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, respiratory airways and lungs, gallbladder, and thymus.
source: However, there are some important differences between taste buds and tuft cells. For example, distinct subsets of taste bud cells express Tas1rs and Tas2rs, which are employed to detect high-energy carbohydrates, nutritious amino acids, or potentially harmful and toxic substances, respectively, conveying the chemical information via different gustatory nerve fibers to the central nervous system, generating hedonic sweet and umami taste perception or unpleasant bitter taste (Doyle et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Tuft cells can sense noxious stimuli and invading pathogens, such as allergens, bacteria, protists, and helminths.
source: These cells can sense noxious stimuli and invading pathogens, such as allergens, bacteria, protists, and helminths (Gerbe et al., 2016; Howitt et al., 2016; Lei et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2019; von Moltke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tuft cells express the sweet and umami taste receptor subunit Tas1r3.
source: Tuft cells are known to express canonical chemosensory signaling pathways, including the sweet and umami taste receptor subunit Tas1r3 (Howitt et al., 2020), bitter taste receptors Tas2rs (Luo et al., 2019; Imai et al., 2020), and olfactory receptors Vmn2r26 (Xiong et al., 2022), as well as their downstream signaling proteins including the heterotrimeric G protein subunits α-gustducin, Gβ1 and Gγ13, phospholipases, and the transient receptor potentialion channel Trpm5 (Howitt et al., 2016; Doyle et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Ablation of α-gustducin or Trpm5 diminishes the intestinal and tracheal epithelia's responses to infection of parasitic helminths and microbial colonization.
source: And ablation of either α-gustducin or Trpm5 diminishes the intestinal and tracheal epithelia's responses to the infection of the parasitic helminths and microbial colonization (Lei et al., 2018; Nadjsombati et al., 2018; Schneider et al., 2018; Keshavarz et al., 2022; Perniss et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tuft cells can release IL-25, prostaglandins, cysteinyl leukotrienes, acetylcholine, and other substances when stimulated.
source: Once stimulated, tuft cells can release a number of output signaling molecules, including IL-25, prostaglandins (Kotas et al., 2022), cysteinyl leukotrienes (Bankova et al., 2018b; Bankova and Boyce, 2018a; McGinty et al., 2020), acetylcholine (Hollenhorst et al., 2020; Krasteva et al., 2011), and other substances, to stimulate type 2 innate lymphoid cells, nerve terminals or adjacent cells, initiating innate and adaptive immune responses, leading to the elimination of irritants and pathogens, and eventually to tissue repair and remodeling (Finger et al., 2003; Tizzano et al., 2010; Saunders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tuft cells are heterogeneous in terms of gene expression patterns, signal transduction pathways, and output effectors.
source: However, tuft cells are heterogeneous in terms of gene expression patterns, signal transduction pathways, and output effectors (Banerjee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Some tuft cells express subsets of Tas2r receptors or cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 3 (Cysltr3) while others do not.
source: For example, some tuft cells express subsets of Tas2r receptors, or cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 3 (Cysltr3) while others do not (Luo et al., 2019; Imai et al., 2020; Bankova et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tuft cells are normally only found in the nasal cavity and trachea, rarely found distal to the lung hilus.
source: Although they are normally only found in the nasal cavity and trachea, rarely found distal to the lung hilus (Krasteva et al., 2011; Tizzano et al., 2010; Saunders et al., 2014), tuft cells can be ectopically formed in the distal lung following severe viral infection or chemical damage (Rane et al., 2019; Barr et al., 2022; Roach et al., 2022; Melms et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tuft cells can be ectopically formed in the distal lung following severe viral infection or chemical damage.
source: Although they are normally only found in the nasal cavity and trachea, rarely found distal to the lung hilus (Krasteva et al., 2011; Tizzano et al., 2010; Saunders et al., 2014), tuft cells can be ectopically formed in the distal lung following severe viral infection or chemical damage (Rane et al., 2019; Barr et al., 2022; Roach et al., 2022; Melms et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and confirmed by data in this study.

claim: Ectopic tuft cells emerge around 12 days post-viral infection.
source: These ectopic tuft cells of molecular diversities emerge around 12 days post-viral infection, suggesting that they may not play any role in the initial response to the infection or during viral clearance (Rane et al., 2019; Barr et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and confirmed by data in this study showing tuft cells at 14 dpi.

claim: Ectopic tuft cells may not play any role in the initial response to infection or during viral clearance.
source: These ectopic tuft cells of molecular diversities emerge around 12 days post-viral infection, suggesting that they may not play any role in the initial response to the infection or during viral clearance (Rane et al., 2019; Barr et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of tuft cell appearance, supported by citations.

claim: H1N1-infected mice showed bodyweight loss with a peak loss of up to 25% around 8-9 days post infection.
source: The mice showed bodyweight loss over the days post-infection with a peak loss of up to 25% of their original bodyweight around 8–9 dpi, and their lungs displayed lesion areas, of which the histological analysis showed massive alveolar damage and severe epithelial dysplasia with altered tissue structures as well as an increased number of CD45+ immune cells in comparison with the uninfected control (Figure 1B, C and D).
evidence: This is supported by bodyweight tracking data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: About 78% of ChAT-expressing cells in H1N1-injured lungs also expressed the tuft cell marker Dclk1.
source: Analysis of the H1N1 injured-lungs of the Chat-Cre: Ai9 mice, which express tdTomato proteins in the ChAT-expressing cells, showed that about 78% of ChAT-expressing cells also expressed the tuft cell marker Dclk1 whereas about 60% and 12% of ChAT-expressing cells expressed the other two taste signaling proteins Gα-gustducin and Plcβ2, respectively (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: Chemically induced severe lung injury with bleomycin, lipopolysaccharide, and house dust mite extracts led to the generation of dysplastic tuft cells.
source: In addition, chemically induced severe lung injury with bleomycin, lipopolysaccharide, and powder of house dust mite extracts also led to the generation of dysplastic tuft cells, but to a lesser extent (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), confirming the severe injury-induced formation of ectopic tuft cells in the lung parenchyma (Rane et al., 2019; Barr et al., 2022; Huang, 2022).

claim: Tas2r105, Tas2r108, Tas2r118, Tas2r137, and Tas2r138 were upregulated in H1N1-infected lungs at 25 dpi compared to 0 dpi.

claim: Subsets of ectopic tuft cells responded to denatonium benzoate and quinine by increasing intracellular calcium concentrations.
source: The results showed that subsets of tuft cells responded to these two compounds by increasing the intracellular calcium concentrations. Application of the bitter taste inhibitor allyl isothiocyanate (AITC), G protein βγ moiety inhibitor gallein or Plcβ2 inhibitor U73122 was able to completely inhibit these cells' calcium responses to the bitter compounds (Figure 2B-K), indicating that the Tas2rs and their downstream signaling proteins are functional in subsets of tuft cells, and may play some physiological roles during the transition from inflammatory response to resolution.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B-K.

claim: WT and Trpm5-/- mice showed similar bodyweight loss/recovery curves with nearly no mortality following H1N1 infection.
source: Results indicated that while WT and Trpm5-/- mice showed similar bodyweight loss/recovery curves with nearly no mortality, Gng13-cKO mice exhibited significantly more bodyweight loss with a maximum of 30% instead of 20% of the original bodyweight, and a slower recovery process with a shifted maximum bodyweight loss from 9 dpi to 10 dpi, and a significant increase in the mortality rate to 37.5%, the majority of which occurred between 8 and 12 dpi (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by bodyweight tracking and survival curve data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Tracheal tuft cells and taste receptor cells in taste buds do not require Trpm5 for their expansion.
source: The proliferation of intestinal tuft cells is dependent on Trpm5 (Howitt et al., 2016; Lei et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2019), but the tracheal tuft cells or sweet, umami, and bitter taste receptor cells in taste buds do not require Trpm5 for their expansion (Damak et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2003; Finger et al., 2005; Hollenhorst et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Trpm5 is not required for the proliferation of dysplastic pulmonary tuft cells.
source: We and others have found that Trpm5 is not required for the proliferation of the dysplastic pulmonary tuft cells (Barr et al., 2022; Huang, 2022), but conditional nullification of Gng13 ablated part of these ectopic tuft cells and reduced the total number of these cells, indicating that different tuft cells utilize different mechanisms to control their proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in this study and citations to prior research.

claim: Different tuft cells utilize different mechanisms to control their proliferation.
source: We and others have found that Trpm5 is not required for the proliferation of the dysplastic pulmonary tuft cells (Barr et al., 2022; Huang, 2022), but conditional nullification of Gng13 ablated part of these ectopic tuft cells and reduced the total number of these cells, indicating that different tuft cells utilize different mechanisms to control their proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of Trpm5 and Gng13 knockout on tuft cell proliferation.

claim: The hyperplasia of intestinal tuft cells and goblet cells is regulated by the Trpm5-IL25-ILC2-IL13 molecular circuit.
source: In the small intestine, the hyperplasia of tuft cells as well as goblet cells is regulated by the Trpm5-IL25-ILC2-IL13 molecular circuit.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about intestinal tuft cell regulation.

claim: Gβγ13 can act on phospholipase Cβ2 or other effectors such as adenylate cyclases, phospholipases, receptor kinases, voltage-gated ion channels, and inward rectifying ion channels.
source: While Gα-gustducin's effectors are still to be determined, Gβγ13 can act on the phospholipase Plcβ2, or other effectors such as adenylate cyclases, phospholipases, receptor kinases, voltage-gated ion channels, and inward rectifying ion channels (Campbell and Smrcka, 2018; Kankanamge et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Plcβ2 can generate the second messengers diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol trisphosphate (IP3).
source: Among them, Plcβ2 can generate the second messengers diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol trisphosphate (IP3) (Huang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: IP3 can bind to and open its channel receptor IP3R on the endoplasmic reticulum, releasing calcium ions and increasing cytosolic calcium concentration.
source: On the other hand, IP3 can bind to and open its channel receptor IP3R on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), releasing the calcium ions from the ER and consequently increasing the cytosolic calcium concentration, leading to the opening of Trpm5, a calcium-activated non-selective monovalent cation channel, depolarizing the membrane potential and releasing certain output signals (Zhang et al., 2007; Liman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The release of IL-25, acetylcholine, ATP, CGRP, and component C3 from tuft cells and taste bud cells is dependent on Trpm5.
source: The release of the cytokine IL-25, acetylcholine (ACh), ATP, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and component C3 from tuft cells and taste bud cells is dependent on Trpm5, but that of some antimicrobial substances and eicosanoids do not require Trpm5 (Lee et al., 2014), indicating that Trpm5 regulates only some output signals' release.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The release of some antimicrobial substances and eicosanoids from tuft cells does not require Trpm5.
source: The release of the cytokine IL-25, acetylcholine (ACh), ATP, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and component C3 from tuft cells and taste bud cells is dependent on Trpm5, but that of some antimicrobial substances and eicosanoids do not require Trpm5 (Lee et al., 2014), indicating that Trpm5 regulates only some output signals' release.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Trpm5-dependent output signaling molecules may not be involved in the regulation of ectopic tuft cells' proliferation.
source: Since the expansion of ectopic tuft cells is independent of Trpm5, we believe that Trpm5-dependent output signaling molecules may not be involved in the regulation of these tuft cells' proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Trpm5 is not required for ectopic tuft cell proliferation.

claim: The effectors activated by the Gβγ13 moiety are involved in the regulation of output signals that promote the proliferation of Gγ13-expressing tuft cells.
source: On the other hand, the elimination of Gγ13-expressing pulmonary tuft cells in the Gng13-cKO mice suggests that the effectors activated by the Gβγ13 moiety are involved in the regulation of output signals that promote the proliferation of Gγ13-expressing tuft cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced number of tuft cells in Gng13-cKO mice.

claim: The differential impact of Trpm5 knockout versus Gng13 abolishment on tuft cell proliferation is probably attributed to Gγ13 being upstream of Trpm5 in the signaling cascades.
source: The differential impact of Trpm5 knockout versus Gng13 abolishment on tuft cell proliferation is probably attributed to the fact that Gγ13 is upstream of Trpm5 in the signaling cascades, thus regulating more signaling pathways, and when mutated, having a more profound effects than Trpm5.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the differential effects.

claim: Elimination of all ectopic tuft cells by knocking out Pou2f3 did not significantly affect the pathogenesis and outcome of H1N1-induced severe injury.
source: Previous reports indicate that the elimination of all ectopic tuft cells by knocking out the Pou2f3 gene did not significantly affect the pathogenesis and outcome of H1N1-induced severe injury (Barr et al., 2022; Huang, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The striking discrepancy between Pou2f3 knockout and Gng13 conditional knockout effects may be caused by the imbalance of tuft cells' diverse functions in the Gng13-cKO lung.
source: The striking discrepancy may be caused by the imbalance of tuft cells' diverse functions in the Gng13-cKO lung.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the different outcomes.

claim: Ectopic tuft cells may not be involved in the initial inflammatory responses to viral infection or the subsequent viral clearance.
source: Since the ectopic tuft cells are absent until 12–14 dpi, these cells may not be involved in the initial inflammatory responses to viral infection or the subsequent viral clearance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of tuft cell appearance.

claim: The missing Gγ13+ tuft cells in Gng13-cKO lungs may play a major role in the transition from inflammatory responses to inflammation resolution and subsequent tissue repair processes.
source: When the pathogeneses enter the later stages, the Gng13-cKO lungs have a much reduced number of tuft cells with only a few of Gγ13-negative tuft cells remaining, leading to much severer symptoms, indicating that the missing tuft cells may play a major role in the transition from the inflammatory responses to inflammation resolution and subsequent tissue repair processes while the remaining tuft cells are unable to effectively contribute to these processes, or even worse, stimulate inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the worse outcomes in Gng13-cKO mice at later time points.

claim: The remaining Gγ13-negative tuft cells in Gng13-cKO lungs are unable to effectively contribute to inflammation resolution and tissue repair, or may even stimulate inflammation.
source: When the pathogeneses enter the later stages, the Gng13-cKO lungs have a much reduced number of tuft cells with only a few of Gγ13-negative tuft cells remaining, leading to much severer symptoms, indicating that the missing tuft cells may play a major role in the transition from the inflammatory responses to inflammation resolution and subsequent tissue repair processes while the remaining tuft cells are unable to effectively contribute to these processes, or even worse, stimulate inflammation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the worse outcomes despite the presence of some tuft cells.

claim: Some tuft cells produce pro-inflammatory cytokines and lipid mediators such as IL-25, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes.
source: Indeed, some tuft cells have been shown to produce pro-inflammatory cytokines and lipid mediators such as IL-25, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes that activate innate and adaptive immune responses (Kotas et al., 2022; Ualiyeva et al., 2021; Hollenhorst and Krasteva-Christ, 2023), and single cell RNAseq analyses indicate that pulmonary ectopic tuft cells express genes that encode enzymes producing specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs), for example, Alox5, Alox12e, Alox15, Ptgs2, encoding arachidonate 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX), arachidonate 12-lipoxygenase (12-LOX), arachidonate 15-lipoxygenase (15-LOX), prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase II (also known as cyclooxygenase II, COX-2), respectively, as well as the genes encoding various isoforms of cytochrome P450: Cyp51, Cyp2f2, Cyp7b1, and Cyp2j6 (Barr et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pulmonary ectopic tuft cells express genes encoding enzymes producing specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs).
source: Indeed, some tuft cells have been shown to produce pro-inflammatory cytokines and lipid mediators such as IL-25, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes that activate innate and adaptive immune responses (Kotas et al., 2022; Ualiyeva et al., 2021; Hollenhorst and Krasteva-Christ, 2023), and single cell RNAseq analyses indicate that pulmonary ectopic tuft cells express genes that encode enzymes producing specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs), for example, Alox5, Alox12e, Alox15, Ptgs2, encoding arachidonate 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX), arachidonate 12-lipoxygenase (12-LOX), arachidonate 15-lipoxygenase (15-LOX), prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase II (also known as cyclooxygenase II, COX-2), respectively, as well as the genes encoding various isoforms of cytochrome P450: Cyp51, Cyp2f2, Cyp7b1, and Cyp2j6 (Barr et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNAseq data cited from prior research.

claim: SPMs can limit further infiltration of neutrophils, recruit and stimulate macrophage phagocytosis, suppress production of pro-inflammatory mediators, increase production of anti-inflammatory mediators, reduce fibrosis, and accelerate tissue repair.
source: These enzymes can utilize membrane lipids such as docosahexaenoid acid, eicosapentaenoid acid and arachidonic acid to biosynthesize SPMs, including lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, and maresins, which can limit further infiltration of neutrophils, recruit and stimulate macrophage phagocytosis to remove dead cells and cell debris, suppress the production of pro-inflammatory mediators and cytokines, and increase the production of anti-inflammatory mediators and cytokines, reduce fibrosis and accelerate tissue repair and remodeling (Serhan et al., 2020; Panigrahy et al., 2021; Serhan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Maresin 1 and resolvin D1 have been shown to inhibit virus- and bacterium-induced inflammation in the lung, respectively.
source: So far, the SPMs maresin 1 and resolvin D1 have been shown to inhibit virus- and bacterium-induced inflammation in the lung, respectively (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2023; Codagnone et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Nullification of Gng13 disrupts the switch from producing proinflammatory lipid mediators to producing anti-inflammatory SPMs.
source: Together, our data from this study implies that nullification of Gng13 not only significantly reduces the number of ectopic tuft cells but also disrupts the switch from producing proinflammatory lipid mediators to producing anti-inflammatory SPMs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and knowledge about tuft cell functions.

claim: The remaining dysplastic tuft cells in Gng13-cKO mice may continue to produce proinflammatory cytokines and lipid mediators whereas the anti-inflammatory agents-producing tuft cells are absent.
source: Given the heterogeneity of tuft cells (Xiong et al., 2022; Bankova et al., 2018b; Haber et al., 2017), we hypothesize that the remaining dysplastic tuft cells may continue to produce proinflammatory cytokines and lipid mediators whereas the anti-inflammatory agents-producing tuft cells are absent in the Gng13-cKO mice, consequently leading to severer outcomes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and knowledge about tuft cell heterogeneity.

claim: Different subtypes of tuft cells may play different subtype-specific roles in the phases of infection, response, resolution, and recovery upon H1N1 infection or other severe injuries.
source: In conclusion, to our knowledge, it is the first time to postulate that different subtypes of tuft cells may play different subtype-specific roles in the phases of infection, response, resolution, and recovery upon H1N1 infection or other severe injuries.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in this study.

claim: Gγ13-expressing ectopic tuft cells promote inflammation resolution and recovery.
source: Our data reveal that Gγ13-expressing ectopic tuft cells promote the inflammation resolution and recovery while other dysplastic lung tuft cells contribute to extended inflammation and perhaps immune storms as well.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing worse outcomes when Gγ13-expressing tuft cells are absent.

claim: Other dysplastic lung tuft cells (Gγ13-negative) contribute to extended inflammation and perhaps immune storms.
source: Our data reveal that Gγ13-expressing ectopic tuft cells promote the inflammation resolution and recovery while other dysplastic lung tuft cells contribute to extended inflammation and perhaps immune storms as well.
evidence: This is speculation based on the worse outcomes in Gng13-cKO mice despite the presence of some tuft cells.
